identity: University of Amsterdam BSc Human Geography and Planning, current ordinary English pathway, retained Planning specialisation, 2026–2027 programme.
controllingSource: Adopted 2026–2027 programme OER B4.2/B4.3/B4.5, dated curriculum 41220 and selected individual course entries.
components: Participate in Thinking Spatially before Research Methods 1. The methods sequence combines qualitative and quantitative social research with GIS.
This 12-credit thematic choice examines property-led urban development, land and property markets, regulation and governance. It requires a positive study recommendation or a completed first year.
Seminar: Planning and Real Estate in Urban Development

This separate six-credit seminar examines planning and real-estate actors, negotiation, redevelopment feasibility and residual land value. It is not a six-credit version of Building the City. A positive first-year study recommendation is required.
Pass Research Methods 1 before Research Methods 2. The latter develops GIS, thematic qualitative analysis and multivariable quantitative analysis.

Pass Academic Skills and the Regional Research Project, and meet the participation requirements in Research Methods 2, before this project. A one- to two-week foreign field visit follows preparation in Amsterdam. Destination and theme are selected from the offered projects.

Pass Academic Skills and meet the Research Methods 2 participation requirements. This four-week project includes a full-time residential fieldwork week in the Netherlands, then quantitative survey analysis and thematic analysis of interviews.
The selected Planning specialisation requires this twelve-credit course in the theories and practices of spatial intervention.

The Planning specialisation also requires this six-credit course on professional planning roles, stakeholder and site analysis and alternative policy actions. Earlier planning theory supplies its preparation.
Urban Planning: Moving in the City
The retained twelve-credit thematic choice studies mobility and spatial development. A positive study recommendation or completed first year is required.
Pass Research Methods 2 and the Netherlands Research Project before Research Methods 3. This course develops the research design and proposal and is normally taken alongside the thesis.

Thirty credits remain open for university bachelor courses, a minor, an approved exchange or an approved internship. Study must take place while enrolled in the degree; vocational higher-education courses do not count. Other arrangements require Examination Board approval.
Bachelor Thesis Project Human Geography & Planning

The twelve-credit thesis is an individual original research project in human geography or planning, supervised within a thematic project group. Pass all first-year courses, Research Methods 2 and the Netherlands Research Project, and meet the participation requirement in Research Methods 3. The latter may run alongside the thesis.

y1-01.name: Introduction to Human Geography
y1-01.entryRequirements: An enrollment in the Bachelor's programme Human Geography and Planning.
y1-01.objectives: At the end of the course: Students can differentiate between the different sub-disciplines and thematic perspectives of Human Geography and the interfaces between them. Students can summarize at elementary level the historical development of Human Geography as a scientific discipline Students can explain geographical meta concepts such as place, space, scale, landscape, clusters, networks, territoriality and borders at an elementary level Students can distinguish the different processes and dimensions of globalization processes Students can recognise how socio-geographical themes are expressed in the Dutch and international context Students can link socio-geographical themes from the scientific literature to social issues and debates at an elementary level Students can identify key concepts and connections between scientific texts on spatial issues and report on them clearly and correctly in writing
y1-01.contents: This course aims to introduce students to Human Geography as a scientific discipline and the way geographers study social issues and processes. Human Geography is a broad and multicoloured discipline. As an 'object study' - a scientific discipline aimed at studying places at different scales - geography is a pluralistic discipline both theoretically and methodologically. This means that geographers analyse places from different theoretical perspectives and with different methods, providing insights into how places differ from each other and are connected at the same time. As spatial scientists, human geographers take an integrative approach: to make sense of developments and changes in neighbourhoods, cities, countries and regions, geographers study how economic, cultural, political and social processes converge in space to give places their own character. At the same time, geographers are mindful of the independent role that place plays in this process of spatial differentiation and specialisation. Place is not simply the outcome of economic, political and socio-cultural activities, but shapes them itself. This interaction between space and social processes - a relationship referred to as spatiality and socio-spatial dialectics - lies at the heart of contemporary geographical approaches. The course Introduction to Human Geography provides students with an overview of the different specialisations and thematic perspectives within Human Geography. During the course, students gain an understanding of core geographical concepts, which underpin spatial analysis, including concepts such as place, space, landscape, scale, globalisation, networks, clusters and territory. The course thus provides a broad basis for choosing different specialisation courses in subsequent years. In addition, seminar sessions train reading and writing skills at academic level on the basis of assignments related to literature on relevant geographical issues.

y1-02.name: Introduction to Spatial Planning
y1-02.entryRequirements: An enrollment in the Bachelor's programme Human Geography and Planning.
y1-02.objectives: This course provides students with an elementary introduction to the planning discipline and the role of planners in urban and regional development. This course contributes to the learning objectives of the Human Geography & Planning bachelor: 1a, 1d, 1i en 1l. The course objectives are the following: Students are able to explain the planning discipline, including the central concepts and methods used by planners, and the changing role of the planner in urban and regional development Students are able to analyse different visions on planning theories and practices, and their interrelationships Students are able to explain the historical development of the planning discipline and the relationships with adjacent scientific disciplines Students are able to explain the changing relationship between state and market, and its implications for planning Students are able to explain the institutional aspects of planning processes, including the changing role of public, private and civic actors Students are able to describe the Dutch and international spatial planning law, in particular the Dutch Environment and Planning Act (Omgevingswet) Students are able to reflect on their assignments based on feedback and peer review
y1-02.contents: Cities and regions are shaped by social, spatial, political and economic dynamics, but also by planning interventions. Spatial planners are key actors in shaping cities and regions. This course will introduce students to the planning discipline, and its changes over time. Firstly, students will gain insights in the shift from modernist, top-down and design-oriented planning approaches to more bottom-up and governance-driven approaches of today. Secondly, students will get to know planning approaches and practices (in particular Dutch practices), and the role of spatial planners in broader governance processes. Thirdly, students will learn how planning theories have evolved over time. Four questions are central in the course: What is planning? Who are planners? What do planners do? How do planners think? Students will develop elementary analytical and critical skills to understand spatial development, as well as creative skills to develop constructive solutions for contemporary challenges for cities and regions. The course consists of two key modules: Foundations of the planning discipline, including its modernist roots; Contemporary challenges for planners. Together, the two modules give students an essential understanding of what the planning discipline entails. Students are encouraged with assignments and observations outside the classroom to see the world through planners' eyes.

y1-03.name: Academic Skills
y1-03.entryRequirements: An enrollment in the Bachelor's programme Human Geography and Planning.
y1-03.objectives: Students are able to comply with the guidelines and regulations regarding plagiarism, ethics and research integrity Students are able to provide constructive feedback to peers, using assessment criteria Students are able to select sources based on relevance, trustworthiness and quality Students are able to understand the relevance of applying apply a social spatial lens to understand a societal issue in practice Students are able to use academic writing conventions Students are able to reflect on their learning process Students are able to identify basic interview techniques
y1-03.contents: This course aims to support students in developing their academic skills and get to know the department and their peers. The first part of the course addresses the core academic skills: academic reporting, critical thinking, reflective practice, project skills and academic citizenship. In the second part students will apply these skills by writing a literature review, developing interview techniques and reflecting on their learning.

y1-04.name: Thinking Spatially
y1-04.entryRequirements: An enrollment in the Bachelor's programme Human Geography and Planning and at the start of the course, participated in Thinking Spatially.
y1-04.objectives: Students are able to explain the position of human geography in relation to planning in the social sciences Students are able to explain the position of spatial planning relation to human geography and other social sciences Students are able to explain the position of socio-spatial research in key debates of philosophies of science Students are able to explain the key components of the social scientific research cycle for qualitative and quantitative methods Students are able to a articulate ethical considerations in conducting social-spatial research Students are able to create simple thematic and planning maps using ArcGIS Pro based on secondary data sources
y1-04.contents: This course sets the scene for understanding and applying research methods in Human Geography and Spatial Planning. It forms the foundation for a series of subsequent courses on research methods and for the bachelor thesis. One part of the course is dedicated to an introduction to the practice of research and to the key approaches in the social sciences, with a specific focus on spatial scientific methods. The second part is dedicated to acquiring skills in Geographical Information System (GIS) – a unique approach and tool for geographers and planners for conducting spatial research. The course consists of introductory lectures accompanied by tutorials, which are followed by practical lab sessions of GIS. The key questions that are discussed during the lectures are: What is social-spatial research? What is unique about spatial research? What is “good” research? How does one get from a research question to an answer? What research designs are commonly used in spatial sciences? What research methods are available to spatial scientists? How does one conduct spatial research ethically?

y1-05.name: Urban Dynamics: Amsterdam in Context
y1-05.entryRequirements: An enrollment in the Bachelor's programme Human Geography and Planning.
y1-05.recommendedPriorKnowledge: Insights from the courses Introduction to Spatial Planning and Introduction to Human Geography (in semester 1).
y1-05.objectives: Students can: Students are able to explain how cities function and how and why they change Students are able to explain how different structural forces cause urban dynamics Students are able to explain the role of spatial interventions, considering how the multi-level nature of structural forces drive urban development Students are able to apply the urban and regional planning perspective to explain different aspects of the study of urban dynamics Students are able to interpret the discipline of human geography as different branch of the social sciences Students are able to apply the geographical perspective to explain different aspects of the study of urban dynamics
y1-05.contents: In this course, students learn to interpret the city and its dynamics. We zoom in on a range of structural forces and conditions ( principia media ) that cause urban dynamics, such as social and economic developments, demographic transitions, global environmental change, technological progress, and changing ideologies of the state. This knowledge is indispensable to explain how cities evolve, and to assess whether it is possible to deliberately intervene in cities changing them towards a new, desired state. The course particularly covers the urban dynamics in Amsterdam, but also considers other international cases. After completing the course, students will have a clear idea of how geographers and planners understand, explain and guide urban dynamics in the contemporary city. The course builds on the introductory courses from semester 1, using concepts such as globalization, place, and space. As the first year of the bachelor programme aims to get students acquainted with the disciplines of human geography and planning, this course provides an introduction to the city as an object of scientific study. The course covers a wide range of topics (e.g., spatial segregation, gentrification, innovative economic milieus, urban mobility, climate mitigation and adaptation), which will be further explored in specialization courses in year 2 and 3.

y1-06.name: Research Methods 1
y1-06.entryRequirements: An enrollment in the Bachelor's programme Human Geography and Planning.
y1-06.objectives: This course consists of two parts: quantitative and qualitative methods. Upon completion of the quantitative part of the course, students will: be familiar with some important quantitative secondary data sources; have the skills to use software for quantitative data processing and analysis (Excel and SPSS); be able to prepare Excel files for use in ArcGIS Pro; be able to perform univariate and bivariate analyses to answer a simple social science research question; will be familiar with the way research results from a random sample can be generalized to the population under study; be able to select the appropriate statistical technique and interpret the result; be able to report the outcome of a statistical analysis through tables, graphs and text Upon completion of the qualitative part of the course, students will: be familiar with typical research question types in qualitative research be familiar with the role of case studies in qualitative research have further developed their skills in preparing for and conducting research interviews This course contributes to following exit qualifications (Dublin Descriptors): Cc, Ce, Ke, Ka, La, Ob Students can identify the level of variables Students are able to explain which statistical analysis technique is appropriate for a basic quantitative problem Students are able to find, retrieve, and handle quantitative databases Students are able to process and descriptively analyse quantitative data using relevant software Students are able to explain basic statistical analyses carried out by others Students are able to report the outcome of statistical analysis Students are able to collect qualitative interview data Students are able to report the outcome of a qualitative analysis
y1-06.contents: Research plays an essential role in understanding, analyzing, and shaping the environments we live in. The course aims to introduce students to the basic quantitative and qualitative research methods and skills needed to conduct solid and meaningful research in the fields of human geography and planning. The first part of the course focuses on quantitative research methods. We build upon the knowledge acquired in the Thinking Spatially course. In the lectures, univariate and bivariate analyses will be introduced. In the computer lab sessions, students will apply univariate and bivariate analyses using Excel and primarily the statistical software IBM SPSS Statistics. Students also learn how to exchange data between Excel, SPSS, and ArcGIS Pro In the second part of the course, the focus is on qualitative methods. We build upon the knowledge acquired in the Academic Skills and Thinking Spatially courses. Attention will be paid to the principles and techniques involved in conducting qualitative case studies and learning the basics of conducting effective interviews, including techniques, question formulation, and ethical considerations.

y1-07.name: Research Project: Regional
y1-07.entryRequirements: An enrollment in the Bachelor's programme Human Geography and Planning.
y1-07.objectives: For this course, students spend a month researching an area in the Randstand, selected by the lecturer, and creating a vision for it. The project proceeds in studio form. Students conduct their own research into the specific area characteristics and are divided into groups that will represent the interests of a stakeholder. They thereby also imagine a vision for the area for 10 years later. How can the area develop in the coming ten years? In Research Project: Regional, students get the chance to apply knowledge gained in the other first year courses in a case from practice, in a group setting. Students are able to develop a scientifically-sound research design based on a geographical-planning problem in a real-world urban development challenge (a case) Students can design an appropriate methodological approach for studying the socio-spatial problem of the case given Students are able to (in groups) develop a creative and realistic urban development vision Students are able to write a report about the results of their analyses Students are able to plan and coordinate data collection and analysis as a group Students are able to argue on behalf of a specific stakeholder Student are able to reflect on the position of different stakeholders and how these shaped their vision Students are able to present their urban development vision in a poster presentation for a non-academic audience
y1-07.contents: In the Amsterdam region, space is scarce and it is important to accommodate developments in the existing built-up area wherever this is possible. Redevelopment creates space to tackle local and regional issues or to develop new ideas. By definition, redevelopment projects are complex tasks involving many different stakeholders, such as housing corporations, the municipality, property developers and residents, each with their own interests, view of the city, and ideas for what needs to be done.

y2-01.name: Urban Planning: Building the City
y2-01.entryRequirements: BSA obtained or first year of a Bachelor's completed.
y2-01.recommendedPriorKnowledge: Ideally students will have taken a first year introductory course on urban planning, or otherwise have a background in the social sciences.
y2-01.objectives: Students will engage in critical discussions and team and individual research, culminating in a comprehensive understanding of what shapes the city between property market dynamics and spatial regulation processes. The lectures will be structured around core themes, with each week dedicated to exploring different aspects of property markets, governance dynamics, planning perspectives, and regulation. This approach aims to provide students with a comprehensive understanding of the multifaceted nature of urban planning and prepare them for the integrative approaches of spatial governance. Students are able to explain the evolution of the field of Urban Governance and Property Development Students are able to analyse a process in the field of Urban Governance and Property Development Students are able to critically reflect on theoretical debates in the field of Urban Governance and Property Development Students are able to explain the evolution of the chosen subdiscipline or subfield of Human Geography or Spatial Planning Students are able to analyse a process in the chosen human geographical subdiscipline or subfield from a socio-spatial perspective Students are able to critically reflect on theoretical debates in the chosen subdiscipline or subfield
y2-01.contents: This course delves into the multifaceted realms of property and urban development through a planning lens, examining the actors, economics, politics, regulation, and governance collectively shaping cities. Specifically, it explores the fundamentals of 'property-led' urban governance and diverse strategies for the production, regulation, and consumption of urban functions. We initiate our journey by analyzing the core principles of property and land development, elucidating their impact on property values and market dynamics in urban development. Subsequently, we investigate the intricacies of regulations, plans, and policies crafted to influence various urban functions ( including housing, retail, workspace, etc). Additionally, we scrutinize measures aimed at addressing environmental and societal imperatives within the framework of property-led urban governance. While the course maintains an international perspective, it grounds its exploration of contemporary Dutch institutions and urban planning paradigms. Beyond offering a critical vantage point, the course fosters a collaborative environment where students not only confront challenges but also explore innovative planning approaches and solutions. The course encompasses a blend of lectures, guest presentations, and interactive sessions, fostering critical discourse and individual research. Through these methods, students develop a holistic understanding of the interplay between property market dynamics and spatial regulation processes in shaping the urban landscape.

y2-02.name: Seminar: Planning and Real Estate in Urban Development
y2-02.entryRequirements: BSA for the Bachelor Human Geography and Planning obtained.
y2-02.objectives: In the course Seminar: Planning and Real Estate in Urban Development the focus will be on the relationship between urban planning and real estate stakeholders in the built environment such as developers, investors, an architects. The courrse will bv gven in English. Students who follow this course will be able to: • to deeply understand what are considerations of different market actors involved in urban development projects; • take a well-considered position on the (spatial) behaviour of different actors involved in urban development projects and how urban planning can negotiate and facilitate; • reflect critically on the functioning of innercity areas and how these areas are being transformed over time following changing urban and retail business trends; • students will get practical knowledge on how to read an urban development plan, on ways to come to residual land value, and learn some basics of rental- and investment value, which are key to link real estate and planning dynamics. Planning–Market Interaction: Explain how planning regulations and market logics shape development feasibility and spatial outcomes in urban projects Actor Roles: Analyse and compare the roles and interests of key actors in urban development processes Risk and Decision-Making: Analyse how market actors assess and manage risk in the real estate development process Application to Planning Practice: Apply knowledge of actor behaviour to analyse negotiation processes in urban development Urban Transformation: Evaluate how planning interventions and real estate dynamics shape urban transformation using empirical observations Feasibility and Valuation: Evaluate urban development proposals using basic feasibility and valuation methods, including residual land value
y2-02.contents: The seminar course Planning and Real Estate in Urban Development is an elective that provides a deeper exploration of key themes in urban development. This course delves into major challenges in Dutch and international urban development, with a particular focus on property markets, retail dynamics, and inner-city development. It examines how these elements shape urban transformations, governance strategies, and spatial planning approaches, equipping students with critical insights into the complexities of contemporary city-building. These include (city centre) retail development and transformation, large scale residential development tasks, and brownfield transformations. Furthermore, students will work with several methods in urban planning including residential land value and defining a development program for a site or redevelopment project. Also, students will get acquainted with negotiation and participation strategies with different actors related to an urban development. The course consists of seven sessions of an interactive nature.

y2-03.name: Research Methods 2
y2-03.objectives: Research Methods 2 enables students to prepare and conduct scientific research independently. Where students were "introduced" to research methods in the first year, we “explore” methodologies to collect data and methodologies for analyses more independently in the second year. In this course, we combine spatial analyses and qualitative and quantitative methodologies. The course combines these research methods and actively encourages students to learn by doing. It helps students independently prepare a research design and conduct research methods that address their research questions. Students are able to explain other researcher's choices for methods and analysis Students are able to substantiate the selection of a research design Students are able to explain theoretical background of key methodological concepts Students are able to apply thematic analysis on text using relevant software Students are able to apply a multivariate analysis of quantitative data with relevant software Students are able to use existing data to test hypotheses Students are able to design survey and interview questions linked to theoretical concepts
y2-03.contents: The GIS section expands on the knowledge gained during the GIS/Cartography section from Methods and Techniques 1. The emphasis is now on learning GIS skills needed to analyze spatial issues in the field. Work is being done on vector and raster data mode, overlay analysis, proximity and range analysis, spatial data collection, and qualitative mapping. In the qualitative methods section, the knowledge gained from M&T1 and Thinking Spatially is further developed as students deepen their interview skills, do ethnographic observations, and start analyzing these qualitative findings using relevant software for coding. During the quantitative section, the following statistical analyses: data preparation and manipulation, causal analysis, and multiple regression analysis.

y2-04.name: Research Project: Abroad
y2-04.entryRequirements: Research Project: Regional completed, Academic Skills completed, and minimum requirements in Research Methods 2 .
y2-04.objectives: Students are able to reflect on to what extent their knowledge applies to a foreign context Students are able to identify how doing research in a foreign context influences the outcomes Students are able to critically reflect on the results of their research in a foreign context Students are able to critically reflect on their own positionality during research in a foreign context Students are able to, in small groups, design, plan and coordinate a research project in an international setting Students are able to coduct a relevant research project in a foreign context
y2-04.contents: Research Abroad consists of a study trip of 1-2 weeks abroad, preceded by a preparatory program in Amsterdam. Students can choose from various destinations, each with specific focus themes. Students first enroll in the course; then (end of semester 1 or beginning of semester 2) an information session follows where the destinations and themes are further explained. Students can then indicate their preferred destination. The program is intensive, both in Amsterdam and during the foreign trip. The program includes: preparatory workshops in Amsterdam, where the research proposal is worked on; a program on-site abroad (lectures, discussions, tours, etc.); and fieldwork assignments during the foreign trip. Students work in small groups on a research theme of their choice, supervised by UvA lecturers and sometimes in collaboration with students and/or lecturers from a local university. The research is concluded with both a scientific research report and a presentation aimed at a broader non-academic audience. The presentations, assignments, and reports are in English.

y2-05.name: Research Project: The Netherlands (English)
y2-05.entryRequirements: A passing grade for Academic Skills and the minimum requirements in Research Methods 2 .
y2-05.requiredPriorKnowledge: A passing grade for Academic Skills and the minimum requirements in Research Methods 2 .
y2-05.objectives: Students are able to collect survey data, in groups and under supervision Students are able to collect interview data in groups and under supervision Students are able to apply thematic analysis to interview data and fieldwork notes with relevant software Students are able to analyse survey data using relevant software Students are able to report clearly and correctly on a concrete spatial issue to an audience of professionals Students are able to reflect on how their own actions and social position influenced the research process and outcomes based on their own fieldwork experiences Students are able to apply research ethics & data integrity guidelines during collaborative fieldwork
y2-05.contents: During the Research Project the students train in collecting and analysing data, and in reporting research findings. The course consists of 4 weeks. Week 1: Preparation for the field work Week 2: Field work. Note: this week requires full time stay on location, including overnight, from Monday morning until Friday evening. Week 3: Quantitative analysis of survey data Week 4: Thematic analysis of interviews, and presentation of results

y2-06.name: Theories of Spatial Interventions
y2-06.recommendedPriorKnowledge: Students should read the literature of the course before each class.
y2-06.objectives: The course introduces students to the different theories and approaches that planners can use to address urgent socio-ecological problems of cities. The course addresses the phylosophical, sociological and political roots of these approaches and engage students with the practice of dealing with concrete plans, policies, and projects. The aim is to ground planning practice in theory and to make planning theory informative for practice. Students are able to critically reflect on different theories and practices of spatial interventions Students are able to evaluate spatial interventions using relevant planning theories Students are able to explain the institutional dimension of planning both in The Netherlands and Internationally (mostly European context) and will be able to compare the difference between different contexts Students are able to reflect on their own positions during the planning process Students are able to evaluate planning problems and the contingencies of complex planning processes Students are able to develop spatial interventions using relevant planning methods
y2-06.contents: Content: In this course students learn about the fundamental models of organizing interventions in space. These forms of collective organization will be firstly explained in theory and then applied to practical examples. In blocks of three weeks, 4 central planning themes will be discussed. In the first week of each theme, theoretical approaches to spatial interventions will be discussed. We will connect works in the sociology and phylosophy of collective action to works on urbanism, design, planning and policy-making anaysis. In week two of each theme, students work on the more practical implications of these theoretical approaches to planning. They will be given concrete problems to solve autonomously, using different forms of knowledge to do so. The themes that will be discussed are: Lecture 1: Introduction Lecture 2: (eco)modernism Lecture 3: strategies Lecture 4: institutions Lecture 5: (post)politics Lecture 6: (de)growth Lecture 7: communication Lecture 8: conflict Lecture 9: exclusion Lecture 10: futures Lecture 11: complexity Lecture 12: DIY urbanism

y2-07.name: Spatial Planning: Theory & Practice
y2-07.entryRequirements: BSA obtained or first year of a Bachelor's completed.
y2-07.recommendedPriorKnowledge: A solid knowledge of planning theory is required, particularly that oriented to various substantive and procedural dilemmas within spatial planning. Familiarity with tendering procedures and local governance issues is a plus, but will also be covered in the course.
y2-07.objectives: This course contributes to the following curriculum objectives: 1a, 1e, 1f, 2b, 2c, 2e, 3a-c, 4a, 4c, 4d, 4f and 5b, 5d, 5e. See also OER article b2.2 (Dublin Descriptors). Students acquire an understanding of planning practice in two contexts: as a policy researcher and as a locally operating planner. Students are able to present their work in an appropriate way to government officials (e.g. in a public procurement procedure) Students are able to explain different roles of planners in professional practice Students are able apply theoretical principles on planning practices Students are able to identify and evaluate different dilemmas in planning practice Students are able to apply a stakeholder analysis Students can formulate an alternative course of action based on a site analysis and evaluation of spatial policies
y2-07.contents: The course Spatial Planning: Theory & Practice is given by two lecturers that, in addition to their employment at the University of Amsterdam, work elsewhere. David Evers is a Senior Researcher at the national government’s Netherlands Environmental Assessment Agency (PBL) and Stan Majoor leads a research programme at the Amsterdam School of Applied Sciences (HvA) which focuses on the role of local planners. The course consists of two separate 3-week modules that are closely linked to the lecturer’s expertise. The two jobs, that of contract researchers / consultants and street-level bureaucrats/frontline planners, are common among UvA graduates. In this way, the course provides insight into what kind of work a student may be doing in a few years.

y3-01.name: Urban Planning: Moving in the City
y3-01.entryRequirements: BSA obtained or first year of a Bachelor's completed.
y3-01.recommendedPriorKnowledge: A background in Social Sciences is recommended to complete the course successfully. Students with other backgrounds are recommended to contact the course coordinator prior to the start of the course to receive preparatory reading material.
y3-01.objectives: In this course, the participants will: explore the key role that mobility plays in the myriad of challenges faced by our cities and societies understand the fundamental relations between mobility systems, mobility behaviour and urban development processes learn to see the positive contributions and potentially perverse effects of mobility innovations apply key principles to challenge the land use and mobility system of cities and regions As a means of attaining these objectives, the participants will: work with typical products of (Dutch and international) planning processes (e.g. mobility and accessibility analyses, masterplans, innovations), and develop a constructive-critical stance towards them. meet and work with practitioners in the domain of mobility and urban development. work in groups and individually to process these lessons into written products and oral presentations. Students know and understand the most important determinants of the relations between land use developments, transport systems, and the behaviour of households and firms. Students know and understand cutting edge national and international examples of planning those systems and can develop a constructive-critical stance on their effectiveness. Students know and understand the key elements and interconnections of different transport and land use systems and can contextualize them to existing cities and regions. Students can report in writing about their position in relation to this knowledge and understanding. Students can constructively-critically reflect on mobility innovations, planning processes and products, as active members of a team. Students can identify mobility challenges and propose/evaluate solution directions, as active members of a team.
y3-01.contents: Mobility forms a core challenge for contemporary society. Urban regions throughout the world — especially rapidly growing ones — are faced with the difficulty of finding a new balance between the positive and negative effects of mobile humans and goods. Moving in the City explains how current mobility problems have been caused and explores ways towards solutions. This module prepares the participant to develop a constructive-critical stance that supports this ongoing search. To this end, the course develops a holistic view on the fundamental interrelations that underlie urban development, individual behaviour and mobility systems. In developing this view, the participant comes to terms with the irreducible complexity and uncertainty that surrounds these domains and their interrelations. Next to conceptual enrichment, the module also focuses on key skills in relation to planning products that influence how we are 'Moving in the City'.

y3-02.name: Research Methods 3
y3-02.entryRequirements: Research Methods 2 and Research Project: The Netherlands (English) /Research Project: The Netherlands (Dutch) completed.
y3-02.requiredPriorKnowledge: This course builds on the knowledge students have acquired in the previous courses Research Methods 1 and 2 and Research Projects Regional and National on different types of research design and methods. Students are expected to take this course concurrently with the Bachelor Thesis Project Human Geography & Planning .
y3-02.objectives: Research Methods 3 prepares students to make relevant choices for the research design and methodology in their research proposal for the bachelor's thesis. It focuses on the importance of a consistent, research approach, methods of data collection and analysis for a scientific production of knowledge And enables students to know why, when and for what specific research methods are used. Students are able to take a position in debates on the philosophy of science Students are able to formulate an appropriate and feasible research question, relevant for societal and/or scientific debates Students are able to write a research proposal for the bachelor thesis in which research question, theory, data and methods are logically interconnected Students are able to apply methods for advanced analysis

y3-04.name: Bachelor Thesis Project Human Geography & Planning
y3-04.entryRequirements: Open to students of the Bachelor's programmes Human Geography and Planning and Beta-Gamma.In addition, students must have successfully completed all first-year courses, as well as Research Methods 2 and Research Project: The Netherlands (Dutch) or Research Project: The Netherlands (English) . Furthermore, students must have met the participation requirement for Research Methods 3 . The course is not open to other students.
y3-04.requiredPriorKnowledge: Students are expected to be familiar with social science research methodology, as taught in the courses Thinking Spatially , Research Methods 1 and 2 , and the Research projects in years 1 and 2 of our Bachelor program.
y3-04.objectives: In this course, students demonstrate that they can bring together academic insights and skills developed throughout their Bachelor program to study a societal issue through a Human Geography or Planning lens by individually conducting, reporting and reflecting on independent and original research. They develop their research within thematically organized project groups under supervision of a daily supervisor, with an individual Bachelor thesis as output. Students can plan and coordinate a research on a relevant topic within scientific debates in Human Geography or Planning Students are able to design a research proposal with a coherent and logical sturcture according to academic writing conventions Students are able to evaluate strong points and points of improvement for their own thesis project Students are able to design and conduct their own research project using research ethics and data integrity guidelines Students are able to to produce an original thesis based on their own research in a well-groomed, coherent and logical structure according to academic writing conventions Students are able to take informed positions in normative and ethical debates based on their own experiences in the thesis project Students are able to design a scientific human geographical or planning research project, under supervision Students are able to independently collect qualitative en of quantitative data fitting the research question Students are able to evaluate the quality of collected data Students are able to evaluate the results of their research Students are able to evaluate the ethical aspects of their research Students are able to analyse a socio-spatial phenomenon from a planning perspective within in a given thesis project Students are able to analyse a socio-spatial process from a geographical perspective within in a given thesis project
y3-04.contents: Thesis projects are offered in both semesters. Themes are communicated via Canvas (after registering) and are offered in both Dutch and English.

findings: Current adopted OER and dated branch tree agree on 60 first-year credits, 24 second-year shared research, 18 Planning and 18 thematic/seminar credits, then 18 thesis/method, 12 thematic and 30 free in year three. The guide introduction retains old two-track/24-specialisation-credit prose. It is not the controlling current table. The three actual specialisations are Human Geography, Planning and Global Urbanism and Transnational Planning. Existing Planning remains a coherent neutral selection; a reordered branch list is not a reason to invalidate it.

The old year-two Contesting the City is absent from that restricted menu, and Building the City is a twelve-credit thematic rather than a six-credit seminar. Corrected to Building the City twelve plus distinct Planning and Real Estate in Urban Development six, linked by actual property/planning substance. Retained current twelve-credit Moving in the City in year three. All require positive BSA or completed first year; the selected seminar explicitly requires BSA. Earlier complete year one meets the ordinary progression. No English/Dutch duplicate Netherlands project is stacked.

First-year Thinking Spatially provides spatial research foundations and ArcGIS maps, then Methods 1 quantitative basics and interview methods. OER requires Thinking Spatially followed for Methods 1; its self-referential participation wording in the Thinking Spatially catalogue is not treated as an impossible self-prerequisite, since the adopted table requires programme enrolment there. Methods 2 requires Methods 1 passed and combines GIS, qualitative coding/interviews and multiple regression. Netherlands fieldwork requires Academic Skills passed and Methods 2 participation/minimum requirements, not prior completion of the whole semester. Its actual periods allow the documented overlap. Abroad requires Regional/Academic Skills passed and Methods 2 participation; ordinary earlier work meets these.

The Netherlands four-week project includes a full-time residential field week, survey analysis and thematic interview analysis. Abroad includes preparation plus one-to-two weeks of foreign field inquiry and English reporting; destination/theme depend on offered projects and remain open. These are required six-credit projects, not exchange space. Methods 3 requires Methods 2 and Netherlands project passed, then supports thesis philosophy, design and proposal. It normally runs alongside the twelve-credit original individual thesis in thematic supervision groups. Thesis requires all year one, Methods 2 and Netherlands passed plus Methods 3 participation, not necessarily Methods 3 passed earlier. No extra dissertation, compulsory internship or invented credit/word threshold is added.

Thirty genuine free credits remain open for academic bachelor courses, a university minor, approved exchange or internship while enrolled. Nonstandard options need Board approval; vocational higher education does not count. No generic FGw introductory-level cap or another degree’s internship limit is imported. Building covers property markets, development and regulation, the separate seminar adds feasibility/land value/actor negotiation, and Moving covers transport, accessibility and land use. The final programme has eighteen components and 180 unique EC.
